turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
This is a really important shift, Ashley. Because beta blockers blunt your heart rate response to exercise, you won't be able to rely on your heart rate or tracker zones to tell you how hard you're working. 

First, you must check in with your doctor or pharmacist to get their specific clearance for lifting and to see if they have any precise limits for you. They are the only ones who can safely clear you for training on this medication.

Once you have their green light, the biggest practical change we'll make is switching our focus entirely to RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) — using a 1-10 scale of how hard the movement actually feels to you, rather than what a watch says. We'll also want to be careful with quick changes in posture (like standing up fast from a heavy squat or deadlift) as beta blockers can make you feel a bit dizzy when you change positions quickly.

Have you had a chance to chat with your doctor about training yet, or are you still waiting to speak with them?

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
When you're lifting on beta blockers, the most noticeable change is that your heart rate simply won't climb the way it used to, even when you are working at your absolute limit. You might feel like you're working at a 9 out of 10 effort, but your tracker might show a heart rate that looks like a warm-up. 

Because of that, here is what to expect and look out for during your sessions:

1. The "ceiling" feeling: You will likely hit a point in your sets where you feel fatigued or out of breath, but your heart rate remains capped. Trust your muscles and your breathing (your RPE) to judge when to stop a set, not your pulse.
2. Postural dizziness: When you transition from lying down or bending over to standing up quickly—like during Romanian deadlifts or coming up from a squat—you might feel a brief lightheadedness. This is very common, so you'll just need to take an extra second or two at the top of those movements to find your footing.
3. Altered recovery between sets: You might find you need slightly longer rest periods to catch your breath, even if your tracker says your heart rate has already recovered. 

It's completely manageable, we just have to play by the body's feedback rather than the numbers on a screen. Have you noticed any of that dizzier feeling when moving around in daily life yet?
